paper.title: The Landscape of the Proximal Point Method for Nonconvex-Nonconcave Minimax Optimization

units.raw_tex: where $L(x,y)$ is a differentiable function in $x$ and $y$.

We say a  function $M(x,y)$ is $\beta$-smooth if its gradient is uniformly $\beta$-Lipschitz
$ \|\nabla M(z) - \nabla M(z')\| \leq \beta\|z-z'\| $
or equivalently for twice differentiable functions, if $\|\nabla^2 M(z)\| \leq \beta$.
Further, we say a twice differentiable $M(x,y)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex-strongly concave for some $\mu\geq 0$ if
$ \nabla^2_{xx} M(z) \succeq \mu I $ and $-\nabla^2_{yy}M(z) \succeq \mu I.$
When $\mu=0$, this corresponds to $M$ being convex with respect to $x$ and concave with respect to $y$.

Notice that the objective $L(x,y)$ is convex-concave when $\rho=0$, and strongly convex-strongly concave when $\rho<0$. Here our primary interest is in the regime where $\rho>0$ is positive, quantifying how nonconvex-nonconcave $L$ is.
In particular, when $\lambda=1$, we recover the traditional PPM \eqref{eq:prox-definition}.

We require that the parameter $\eta$ is selected with $\eta > \rho$, which ensures the minimax problem in~\eqref{eq:saddle-envelope} is strongly convex-strongly concave. As a result, the saddle envelope is well-defined (as its subproblem has a unique minimax point) and often can be efficiently approximated.

statement.raw_tex:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:two-sided-dominance}
	For any objective $L$ that is $\rho$-weakly convex-weakly concave and $\alpha > 0$-interaction dominant in both $x$ and $y$, the damped PPM~\eqref{eq:saddle-PPM} with $\eta$ and $\lambda$ satisfying
	$$ \lambda \leq 2\frac{\min\left\{1,(\eta/\rho-1)^2\right\}}{\eta/\alpha+1} $$
	linearly converges to the unique stationary point $(x^*,y^*)$ of~\eqref{eq:main-problem} with
	$$\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_k-x^* \\ y_k-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 \leq \left(1 - \frac{2\lambda}{\eta/\alpha+1} + \frac{\lambda^2}{\min\left\{1,(\eta/\rho-1)^2\right\}}\right)^{k}\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_0-x^* \\ y_0-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2.$$
	For example, setting $\eta=2\rho$ and $\lambda=\frac{1}{1+\eta/\alpha} $, our convergence rate simplifies to
	$$\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_k-x^* \\ y_k-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 \leq \left(1-\frac{1}{(2\rho/\alpha+1)^2} \right)^{k}\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_0-x^* \\ y_0-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2.$$
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma} \label{lem:helper0}
	Suppose $M(x,y)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex-strongly concave on a convex set $S=S_x\times S_y$, then it holds for any $(x,y),(x',y') \in S$ that
	$$\mu\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x-x' \\ y-y' \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 \leq \left(\begin{bmatrix} \nabla_x M(x,y)  \\-\nabla_y M(x,y) \end{bmatrix} -\begin{bmatrix} \nabla_x M(x',y')  \\-\nabla_y M(x',y') \end{bmatrix}\right)^T\begin{bmatrix} x-x' \\ y-y' \end{bmatrix}.$$
	When $\nabla M(x', y')=0$, the distance to this stationary point is bounded by
	$$
	\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x-x' \\ y-y' \end{bmatrix}\right\| \leq \frac{\|\nabla M(x,y)\|}{\mu} \ . 
	$$
\end{lemma}

egin{proof}
	First consider any stationary point $z=(x,y)$ of $L$. Denote $z_+=\prox_\eta(z)$ and the objective function defining the proximal operator~\eqref{eq:prox-definition} as $M(u,v) = L(u,v) +  rac{\eta}{2}\|u-x\|^2- rac{\eta}{2}\|v-y\|^2$. Then observing that $
abla M(z)=0$, $z$ must be the unique minimax point of $M$ (that is, $z=z_+=\prox_\eta(z)$). Hence $z$ must be a stationary point of $L_\eta$ as well since $
abla L_\eta(z) =
abla L(z_+)=
abla L(z)= 0$.
	
	Conversely consider a stationary point $z=(x,y)$ of $L_\eta$. Then $\eta(x-x_+) = 
abla_x L_\eta(z)=0$ and $\eta(y_+-y) = 
abla_y L_\eta(z)=0$. Hence we again find that $z=z_+=\prox_\eta(z)$ and consequently, this point must be a stationary point of $L$ as well since $
abla L(z)=
abla L(z_+)=
abla L_\eta(z)=0$.
\end{proof}

	Recall Lemma~ef{lem:grad-formula} showed the gradient of the saddle envelope is given by $
abla_x L_\eta(z) = \eta(x-x_+)$ and $
abla_y L_\eta(z) = \eta(y_+-y)$. Applying this at $z$ and $z_+$ and dividing by $\eta$, our claimed Hessian formula becomes

	 egin{bmatrix} x^\Delta_+-x_+\ y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} = \eta\left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -

	Our proof shows this in two steps: first considering a proximal step on the second-order Taylor approximation of $L$ at $z_+$ and then showing this closely matches the result of a proximal step on $L$.
	
	First, consider the following quadratic model of the objective around $z_+$:
	$$ \widetilde L(z) = L(z_+) + 
abla L(z_+)^T(z-z_+) +  rac{1}{2}(z-z_+)^T
abla^2 L(z_+)(z-z_+) \ . $$
	Denote the result of one proximal step on $\widetilde L$ from $z^\Delta$ by $\widetilde z^\Delta_+ = (\widetilde x_+^\Delta, \widetilde y_+^\Delta)$. Since the proximal subproblem is strongly convex-strongly concave, this solution is uniquely determined by

	This is nearly our target condition~\eqref{eq:target-hessian-condition}. All that remains is to show our second-order approximation satisfies $\| z^\Delta_+ - \widetilde z^\Delta_+\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$.
	Denote the proximal subproblem objective by $ M^\Delta (u,v) = L(u,v) +  rac{\eta}{2}\|u-x^\Delta\|^2 -  rac{\eta}{2}\|v-y^\Delta\|^2$ and its approximation by $\widetilde M^\Delta (u,v) = \widetilde L(u,v) +  rac{\eta}{2}\|u-x^\Delta\|^2 -  rac{\eta}{2}\|v-y^\Delta\|^2$.
	Noting that $\|
abla \widetilde M^\Delta (x_+,y_+)\| = \eta\|\Delta\|$, we can apply Lemma~ef{lem:helper0} to the $(\eta-ho)$-strongly convex-strongly concave function $\widetilde M^\Delta$ to bound the distance to its minimax point as
	$$ \|z_+-\widetilde z_+^\Delta\|\leq  rac{\eta}{\eta-ho}\|\Delta\| \ .$$
	Consequently, we can bound difference in gradients between $L$ and its quadratic model $\widetilde L$ at $\widetilde z^\Delta_+$ by $ \|
abla L(\widetilde z^\Delta_+) - 
abla \widetilde L(\widetilde z^\Delta_+)\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$. Therefore $\|
abla M^\Delta(\widetilde z^\Delta_+)\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$ and so applying Lemma~ef{lem:helper0} to the strongly convex-strongly concave function $M^\Delta$ bounds the distance to its minimax point as $\|z^\Delta_+ - \widetilde z^\Delta_+\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$, which completes our proof.

Lemma~\ref{lem:helper1} ensures the existence of a nearby stationary point $(x^*,y^*)$. Then the standard proof for strongly monotone (from Lemma~\ref{lem:helper0}) and Lipschitz operators gives a contraction whenever $s\in(0, 2\mu/\beta^2) $:
\begin{align*}
\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k+1}-x^* \\ y_{k+1}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2
&= \left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k}-x^* \\ y_{k}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 - 2s\begin{bmatrix} \nabla_x M(x_k,y_k) \\ -\nabla_y M(x_k,y_k) \end{bmatrix}^T\begin{bmatrix} x_k-x^* \\ y_k-y^* \end{bmatrix} + s^2\left\|\begin{bmatrix} \nabla_x M(x_k,y_k) \\ -\nabla_y M(x_k,y_k) \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2\\
&\leq \left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k}-x^* \\ y_{k}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 - 2\mu s\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k}-x^* \\ y_{k}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 + \beta^2s^2\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k}-x^* \\ y_{k}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2\\
&= \left(1 - 2\mu s+\beta^2s^2\right)\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k}-x^* \\ y_{k}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2 \ , 
\end{align*}
where the inequality utilizes \eqref{eq:lemA2.2} at $(x,y)=(x_k,y_k)$ and the smoothness of $M(x,y)$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:helper1} ensures the existence of a nearby stationary point $(x^*,y^*)$. Then the standard proof for strongly monotone (from Lemma~\ref{lem:helper0}) and Lipschitz operators gives a contraction whenever $s\in(0, 2\mu/\beta^2) $:

\left\|\begin{bmatrix} x_{k+1}-x^* \\ y_{k+1}-y^* \end{bmatrix}\right\|^2

egin{proof}
	Consider some $z=(x,y)$ and a nearby point $z^\Delta=z+\Delta$. Denote one proximal step from each of these points by $z_+=(x_+,y_+)= \prox_\eta(z)$ and $z^\Delta_+=(x^\Delta_+,y^\Delta_+)= \prox_\eta(z^\Delta)$. 
	Then our claimed Hessian formula amounts to showing
	 egin{align*}
		 egin{bmatrix} 
abla_x L_\eta(z^\Delta) \ -
abla_y L_\eta(z^\Delta) \end{bmatrix} -  egin{bmatrix} 
abla_x L_\eta(z) \ -
abla_y L_\eta(z) \end{bmatrix}  &= \left(\eta I - \eta^2\left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix}ight)^{-1}ight) egin{bmatrix} \Delta_x\ \Delta_y  \end{bmatrix} +o(\|\Delta\|).
	\end{align*}
	Recall Lemma~ef{lem:grad-formula} showed the gradient of the saddle envelope is given by $
abla_x L_\eta(z) = \eta(x-x_+)$ and $
abla_y L_\eta(z) = \eta(y_+-y)$. Applying this at $z$ and $z_+$ and dividing by $\eta$, our claimed Hessian formula becomes
	 egin{equation} \label{eq:target-hessian-condition}
	 egin{bmatrix} x^\Delta_+-x_+\ y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} = \eta\left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix}ight)^{-1} egin{bmatrix} \Delta_x\ \Delta_y \end{bmatrix} +o(\|\Delta\|) \ .
	\end{equation}
	Our proof shows this in two steps: first considering a proximal step on the second-order Taylor approximation of $L$ at $z_+$ and then showing this closely matches the result of a proximal step on $L$.
	
	First, consider the following quadratic model of the objective around $z_+$:
	$$ \widetilde L(z) = L(z_+) + 
abla L(z_+)^T(z-z_+) +  rac{1}{2}(z-z_+)^T
abla^2 L(z_+)(z-z_+) \ . $$
	Denote the result of one proximal step on $\widetilde L$ from $z^\Delta$ by $\widetilde z^\Delta_+ = (\widetilde x_+^\Delta, \widetilde y_+^\Delta)$. Since the proximal subproblem is strongly convex-strongly concave, this solution is uniquely determined by
	$$
	 egin{bmatrix} 
abla_x \widetilde L(\widetilde x^\Delta_+,\widetilde y^\Delta_+)\  -
abla_y \widetilde L(\widetilde x^\Delta_+,\widetilde y^\Delta_+)\end{bmatrix} +  egin{bmatrix} \eta(\widetilde x^\Delta_+-x^\Delta)\ \eta(\widetilde y^\Delta_+-y^\Delta) \end{bmatrix} = 0 \ .
	$$
	Plugging in the definition of our quadratic model $\widetilde L$ yields
	 egin{align*}
	& egin{bmatrix} 
abla_x L(z_+)\ -
abla_y L(z_+)\end{bmatrix} +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} \widetilde x^\Delta_+-x_+\ \widetilde y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} +  egin{bmatrix} \eta(\widetilde x^\Delta_+-x^\Delta)\ \eta(\widetilde y^\Delta_+-y^\Delta) \end{bmatrix} = 0 \ .
	\end{align*}
	Hence
	 egin{align*}
	& \left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix}ight) egin{bmatrix} \widetilde x^\Delta_+-x_+\  \widetilde y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} = \eta  egin{bmatrix} x^\Delta - x_+ -\eta^{-1}
abla_x L(z_+) \ y^\Delta - y_+ +\eta^{-1}
abla_y L(z_+) \end{bmatrix}\
	&\implies  \left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix}ight) egin{bmatrix} \widetilde x^\Delta_+-x_+\  \widetilde y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} = \eta  egin{bmatrix} \Delta_x\ \Delta_y \end{bmatrix}\
	&\implies   egin{bmatrix} \widetilde x^\Delta_+-x_+\ \widetilde y^\Delta_+-y_+ \end{bmatrix} = \eta\left(\eta I +  egin{bmatrix} 
abla^2_{xx} L(z_+) & 
abla^2_{xy} L(z_+)\  -
abla^2_{yx} L(z_+) & -
abla^2_{yy} L(z_+)\end{bmatrix}ight)^{-1} egin{bmatrix} \Delta_x\ \Delta_y \end{bmatrix}.
	\end{align*}
	
	This is nearly our target condition~\eqref{eq:target-hessian-condition}. All that remains is to show our second-order approximation satisfies $\| z^\Delta_+ - \widetilde z^\Delta_+\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$.
	Denote the proximal subproblem objective by $ M^\Delta (u,v) = L(u,v) +  rac{\eta}{2}\|u-x^\Delta\|^2 -  rac{\eta}{2}\|v-y^\Delta\|^2$ and its approximation by $\widetilde M^\Delta (u,v) = \widetilde L(u,v) +  rac{\eta}{2}\|u-x^\Delta\|^2 -  rac{\eta}{2}\|v-y^\Delta\|^2$.
	Noting that $\|
abla \widetilde M^\Delta (x_+,y_+)\| = \eta\|\Delta\|$, we can apply Lemma~ef{lem:helper0} to the $(\eta-ho)$-strongly convex-strongly concave function $\widetilde M^\Delta$ to bound the distance to its minimax point as
	$$ \|z_+-\widetilde z_+^\Delta\|\leq  rac{\eta}{\eta-ho}\|\Delta\| \ .$$
	Consequently, we can bound difference in gradients between $L$ and its quadratic model $\widetilde L$ at $\widetilde z^\Delta_+$ by $ \|
abla L(\widetilde z^\Delta_+) - 
abla \widetilde L(\widetilde z^\Delta_+)\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$. Therefore $\|
abla M^\Delta(\widetilde z^\Delta_+)\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$ and so applying Lemma~ef{lem:helper0} to the strongly convex-strongly concave function $M^\Delta$ bounds the distance to its minimax point as $\|z^\Delta_+ - \widetilde z^\Delta_+\| = o(\|\Delta\|)$, which completes our proof.
\end{proof}

source_units.raw_tex:
We say a  function $M(x,y)$ is $\beta$-smooth if its gradient is uniformly $\beta$-Lipschitz
$ \|\nabla M(z) - \nabla M(z')\| \leq \beta\|z-z'\| $
or equivalently for twice differentiable functions, if $\|\nabla^2 M(z)\| \leq \beta$.
Further, we say a twice differentiable $M(x,y)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex-strongly concave for some $\mu\geq 0$ if
$ \nabla^2_{xx} M(z) \succeq \mu I $ and $-\nabla^2_{yy}M(z) \succeq \mu I.$
When $\mu=0$, this corresponds to $M$ being convex with respect to $x$ and concave with respect to $y$.
